system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2193-01-28 17:52:00 to 2193-01-29 17:12:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with end-stage liver disease from hepatitis C and hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for altered mental status and a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure with a focal onset. Initial concerns included infection, metabolic derangements, and intracranial pathology. Workup revealed hyponatremia, markedly elevated blood glucose leading to a new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, and a urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. A non-contrast head CT and MRI showed no acute intracranial abnormality, though EEG indicated diffuse encephalopathy. Lumbar puncture, performed after correction of coagulopathy, ruled out central nervous system infection. The patient improved with antibiotics, insulin, lactulose, and levetiracetam. She was discharged to extended care with stable vital signs, resolved infection, and improved mental status, on a regimen including insulin, Keppra, and lactulose, with plans for neurology, endocrinology, and liver follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I went to my rehab appointment this morning. I had breakfast and took my insulin, but then I started feeling really groggy in the waiting room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood sugar was 42 when they checked it. That’s quite low. Did you lose consciousness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t pass out, but I was very drowsy. They gave me some juice and I felt a bit better, but still weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Low blood sugar can cause that. We’ve admitted you so we can adjust your insulin and make sure nothing else is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My sugars have been all over the place since I started insulin. I’m worried I’ll have another episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to lower your insulin dose to 8 units twice daily instead of 16. That should help prevent lows. We’ll also monitor your sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve also been feeling weaker than usual. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weakness is likely due to your chronic liver disease. We did notice mild asterixis—flapping tremor in your hands—which can be a sign of early hepatic encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I had confusion and a seizure. Could this be leading to that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a head CT and it showed no acute issues. Your seizure is still well-controlled on Keppra. But we are keeping you on lactulose to help clear toxins from your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in a day. Could that be making things worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we gave you a lactulose enema earlier. You were able to go, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I did. I actually feel a little sharper now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also found signs of a urinary tract infection—bacteria and nitrates in your urine. You got IV cipro in the ER and will continue oral cipro for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t have burning or urgency. Is it still serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious, but we treat it because with your liver disease, infections can worsen confusion or weakness. We’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs improved—liver enzymes are coming down, sugars are stable in the 100s, and your infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my anemia? My hematocrit dropped a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still within your usual range. You mentioned some vaginal bleeding a few days ago—resolved now. But you should discuss that with your primary doctor at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. So I’m okay to go back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re stable, afebrile, and your condition has improved. We’re discharging you to the extended care facility with adjusted insulin and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking all my other meds—lactulose, Keppra, the blood pressure ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Continue everything as prescribed. Watch for fevers, confusion, trouble urinating, or low sugars. Call your doctor if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing my insulin is adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep up with your follow-ups with neurology, endocrinology, and liver clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip back. We’ll send all the details to your rehab team.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with end-stage liver disease from hepatitis C and a recent history of seizure and new-onset diabetes, was admitted for hypoglycemia and generalized weakness. She developed low blood sugar during a rehab appointment despite taking her usual insulin dose, prompting evaluation. Workup revealed stable chronic anemia, elevated liver enzymes that improved during the stay, and a urinary tract infection detected on urinalysis. A non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial process. Her insulin dose was reduced from 16 to 8 units twice daily to prevent further hypoglycemia, and she was continued on lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy, with improvement after a lactulose enema. She received ciprofloxacin for the UTI and remained hemodynamically stable. She was discharged to extended care with stable glucose levels, resolved encephalopathy symptoms, and a plan to continue all medications, including adjusted insulin, antibiotics, and neurologic and liver support therapies.
